title: Dealing with asbestos and RCS
summary: Explains what asbestos is, where it may be found and what to do if you suspect it, plus the dangers of respirable crystalline silica (RCS) dust and the precautions for electrical workers.

sections.heading: What asbestos is
paragraphs: Asbestos is a fibrous material that is opencast mined from the ground. It is no longer used, but it was used extensively in the construction industry in the past, particularly in homes built or refurbished between 1950 and 1980.

sections.heading: Effects of asbestos on health
paragraphs: The tiny fibres pass into the lower parts of the lung, where they can remain for years. The delay between first exposure and the start of a disease can vary from 15 to 60 years.
In some cases the fibres can work through the lung lining. Asbestos cannot be absorbed through your skin.
bullets: Conditions caused: lung cancer, mesothelioma and asbestosis
Delay between exposure and disease: 15 to 60 years
Asbestos cannot be absorbed through the skin

sections.heading: Where asbestos might be found
paragraphs: Asbestos was used in a wide variety of building applications.

sections.heading: If you suspect asbestos
paragraphs: Assume that anything that looks like asbestos is asbestos. If you are in any doubt about whether the material you are working with contains asbestos, stop work immediately and find out.
If you have come into direct contact with the material, remove outer clothing such as overalls and tee shirt, place it in a sealed plastic bag for disposal, and wash yourself thoroughly.
bullets: For non-domestic premises, the owner/occupier should have an asbestos survey/register, which should be referred to before any work starts
The person in charge of the job must investigate whether there is any asbestos on site

sections.heading: Disposing of asbestos
paragraphs: The Control of Asbestos Regulations cover all aspects of dealing with asbestos. Asbestos is hazardous waste, so it must be packaged and labelled as such and taken to a licensed waste disposal site.
bullets: The Regulations cover identifying the problems, the responsibilities of property owners, employer and employee responsibilities, and removal and disposal
Packaged and labelled as hazardous waste
Taken to a licensed waste disposal site

sections.heading: Silica, RCS and silicosis
paragraphs: What we commonly call dust in construction is often Respirable Crystalline Silica (RCS). It is found in stone, rocks, sands and clays.

Long exposure to RCS can cause fibrosis (hardening or scarring) of the lung tissue with a loss of lung function. The effect continues to develop after exposure has stopped and is irreversible. Sufferers usually become house-bound or even bed-bound.
bullets: Source of these figures: HSE web site

sections.heading: Silicosis risks for electrical engineers
paragraphs: Electricians face an immediate risk of inhaling RCS when drilling or cutting (chasing out) brick, concrete and similar materials, and when working on a site where other trades are creating large amounts of dust containing RCS.
bullets: Report issues such as having to work where airborne dust is present
If in doubt, stop work and move away
The HSE has a guide for employees available on its web site

flashcards.front: Name the three main types of asbestos and their common colours.
In which homes was asbestos used most extensively?
flashcards.back: Homes built or refurbished between 1950 and 1980.

flashcards.front: What diseases can asbestos fibres cause?
How long can the delay be between asbestos exposure and disease?
Can asbestos be absorbed through the skin?
flashcards.back: No. The danger comes from fibres passing into the lower parts of the lung.

flashcards.front: Where might asbestos be found in a building?
flashcards.back: Steel frames, guttering, rainwater pipework, boiler insulation, pipe lagging, wall, ceiling and door lining, corrugated roofing, and ceiling and floor tiles.

flashcards.front: What should you assume about material that looks like asbestos?
flashcards.back: Assume that anything that looks like asbestos is asbestos. If in any doubt, stop work immediately and find out.

flashcards.front: What should you do if you come into direct contact with suspected asbestos?
flashcards.back: Remove outer clothing such as overalls and tee shirt, place it in a sealed plastic bag for disposal, and wash yourself thoroughly.

flashcards.front: What should the owner/occupier of non-domestic premises have for asbestos?
flashcards.back: An asbestos survey/register, which should be referred to before the start of any work.

flashcards.front: How must asbestos waste be handled?
flashcards.back: It is hazardous waste: packaged and labelled as such and taken to a licensed waste disposal site.
Respirable Crystalline Silica, found in stone, rocks, sands and clays and often what is commonly called dust in construction.

flashcards.front: What does long-term RCS exposure do to the lungs?
flashcards.back: Causes fibrosis (hardening or scarring) of lung tissue and loss of lung function. It keeps developing after exposure stops and is irreversible.

flashcards.front: What should you do if you must work where airborne dust is present and you are in doubt?
flashcards.back: Report the issue, stop work and move away, and always wear appropriate protective equipment.

quiz.q: Which type of asbestos is known as blue asbestos?
quiz.why: Crocidolite is blue asbestos, amosite is brown and chrysolite is white.

quiz.q: How long can the delay between first exposure to asbestos and the start of disease be?
quiz.why: The delay between first exposure and the start of a disease can vary from 15 to 60 years.

quiz.q: Which statement about asbestos is correct?
options: It can be absorbed through your skin
It cannot be absorbed through your skin
It only harms people who eat it
quiz.why: Asbestos cannot be absorbed through your skin; the fibres pass into the lower parts of the lung.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a condition caused by asbestos fibres?
quiz.why: Lung cancer, mesothelioma and asbestosis are the conditions listed for asbestos fibres; silicosis is caused by silica.

quiz.q: You are working with a material you are not sure contains asbestos. What must you do?
options: Stop work immediately and find out
Sweep it up and bin it
quiz.why: If in any doubt about asbestos, stop work immediately and find out; assume anything that looks like asbestos is asbestos.

quiz.q: You have come into direct contact with suspected asbestos material. What should you do with your overalls and tee shirt?
options: Place them in a sealed plastic bag for disposal
Wash them with your own clothes
Wear them home and wash them there
quiz.why: Remove outer clothing, place it in a sealed plastic bag for disposal and wash yourself thoroughly.

quiz.q: Before work starts in non-domestic premises, what document should be referred to for asbestos information?
quiz.why: The owner/occupier of non-domestic premises should have an asbestos survey/register, which should be referred to before any work starts.

quiz.q: Where must asbestos waste be taken?
quiz.why: Asbestos is hazardous waste and must be packaged and labelled as such and taken to a licensed waste disposal site.

quiz.q: What is respirable crystalline silica (RCS) commonly mistaken for in construction?
quiz.why: What we commonly simply call dust in construction is often RCS.

quiz.q: Which building material contains the widest range of silica, from 25% to 70%?
quiz.why: Concrete and mortar contain 25% - 70% silica; brick is up to 30% and slate up to 40%.

options: It always clears up after exposure ends
The effect continues to develop after exposure has stopped and is irreversible
quiz.why: The lung scarring continues to develop after exposure has stopped and cannot be reversed.

quiz.q: Which task poses an immediate risk of inhaling RCS for an electrician?
options: Drilling or chasing out brick or concrete
quiz.why: Drilling or cutting (chasing out) brick, concrete and similar materials creates an immediate risk of inhaling RCS.
